title: Battles in the Supreme Court -- Ch. 4: BATTLES OVER LIFE AND DEATH

primary_topics: Chapter 4 of 'Battles in the Supreme Court' -- CJP's account of the Court's battles over the death penalty: the constitutionality of RA 7659 upheld 12-3 in Echegaray, the question whether an escaped appellant's death sentence must still be reviewed, the fight over repetitive dissents, and the challenge to the Lethal Injection Law

The constitutional argument he reproduces at length: Section 19, Article III abolished the death penalty and allowed its restoration only 'for compelling reasons involving heinous crimes,' a duty Congress did not discharge by merely reimposing death on crimes already punishable by death

The moral and practical case against capital punishment -- its heavier fall on the poor and unlettered, the Constitution's 'explosion of concern for man more than property,' and the Church's limitation of the penalty to cases of absolute necessity in Evangelium Vitae

The dissenters' insistence on their right to repeat their negative votes in every death case, ending in the compromise clause reproduced in all future affirmations, and his prediction that 'eventually, the dissenters will win'

His closing personal verdict: the death penalty is not per se objectionable but should be prescribed only for a very limited number of truly heinous crimes, because in an imperfect judicial system an innocent man could be executed through plain human error
sub_topics: The framing and the constraint: with the Cha-cha cases past, death cases now occupy the Court and the public; by Court tradition these decisions and opinions are per curiam, so he will name neither ponentes nor dissenters even though he personally disagrees with the practice

The constitutional text and the statute: Section 19, Article III bars the death penalty 'unless for compelling reasons involving heinous crimes, the Congress hereafter provides for it'; Congress provided for it in RA 7659, effective December 31, 1993, after which trial courts imposed at least 748 death sentences, growing by about thirteen a month

Echegaray: the Court upheld the constitutionality of RA 7659 by 12 to 3 in a per curiam Resolution of February 7, 1997, on a Supplemental Motion for Reconsideration raised only at that stage by new counsel from the Free Legal Assistance Group

The majority's four reasons: death is not cruel, unjust, excessive or unusual but an expression of the state's prerogative to secure society against threatened and actual evil; the covered offenses satisfy the element of heinousness; the law is replete with procedural and substantive safeguards; and the Constitution does not require statistical proof of a higher incidence of crime before death may be prescribed

The first, three-page Dissent: a 'marked change in the milieu' from the Constitution's adoption to the statute's enactment was required, a milieu that 'must have turned from bad to worse,' and the heinous nature of the crimes had not been shown to be exceptionally offensive

The second, 32-page Dissent reproduced at length: Congress merely amended provisions of the Revised Penal Code, added an article and amended special laws without changing the nature or elements of the crimes -- it 'merely made the penalty more severe' -- and so failed its specific and positive constitutional duty

The constitutional history invoked: the phrase 'unless for compelling reasons involving heinous crimes' was introduced by Commissioner Christian Monsod, and the commissioners' examples were 'organized murder' and the 'brutal murder of a rape victim,' not offenses already penalized with death

The three-part test of heinousness proposed by the dissent -- entirely new offenses of unheard-of perversity, existing crimes with a new element such as 'organized' or 'brutal,' or a means or method evincing extreme violence, cruelty and atrocity

CJP's own interjection in his own voice that there are too many crimes to which death has been prescribed, more capital crimes now than before the 1987 Constitution, which partly accounts for the unusually large number of death sentences

The deterrence debate and the pro-life Constitution: no empirical proof links prescribing death to the commission or non-commission of crimes, while the Charter's guarantees of dignity, human rights, the life of the mother and the unborn, health, ecology and education amount to a constitutional explosion of concern for man more than property
The class argument: death 'militated against the poor and powerless,' almost all of those sentenced being underprivileged, breeding in them a sense of the unequal balance of the scales of justice

The dissent's six-point epilogue: the Constitution abolished rather than suspended the death penalty, granted a new right against it as a species of the right to life, required strict construction of any reviving law, treated every constitutional word as sacred, imposed two concurrent requirements of attendant circumstances and post-ratification compelling reasons, and demanded that heinousness be shown crime by crime -- reinforced by 'Thou shall not kill' and Pope John Paul II's Evangelium Vitae

People v. Esparas: whether the Court should automatically review a death sentence when the appellant has escaped; six justices held existing jurisprudence required review regardless, CJP and Justice Vitug joined only in the result and would not render judgment until rearrest, and seven dissenters said the escapee relinquished the protection of the judiciary; the issue became academic when Esparas was rearrested

People v. Prades: the issue resurfaced, and all but one justice held that the Court can validly promulgate judgment despite the escape, so that the judicial process is not subverted by an accused jumping bail -- with the lone dissenter restating that the Court should not deliberate or render judgment until rearrest or voluntary submission

Repetitive dissents: after a long roll of affirmed death sentences, the majority in People v. Escala objected that repeated dissents undermined the judicial process in the eyes of trial judges required to impose the penalty; the minority defended the right to dissent repetitively while submitting to the ruling, and the compromise was a final Dissenting Opinion in Escala plus a standard clause reproduced in all future affirmations, by which time the dissenters had grown from three to four

The Escala dissent reproduced verbatim: asked by colleagues to stop voting against death for the sake of unanimity, the dissenter refused after 'soul-searching, reflection and prayer,' insisting that every review is de novo, warning that affirmances could mean one convict put to death every working day -- 'a massacre more gruesome than the AIDS epidemic and the Cambodian killing fields' -- and vowing to keep voting against every death penalty

The Lethal Injection Law: electrocution gave way to gas poisoning under RA 7659, then to lethal injection under RA 8177 after the electric chair burned and a gas chamber proved too expensive; FLAG's Anti-Death Penalty Task Force, led by Atty. Theodore Te for Leo Echegaray, attacked RA 8177 on six grounds

The 10-4 ruling in Echegaray v. Secretary of Justice: the law was upheld but Sections 17 and 19 of its implementing rules were struck down -- the three-year reprieve for a married woman ignored Article 83 of the Revised Penal Code, and the confidentiality of the execution manual denied access to matters of public concern; the Court also described the three-drug protocol, found it not to involve torture or a lingering death under Harden, and held the delegation to the justice secretary and the Bureau of Corrections valid

The four dissents on lethal injection: one that the invalidity of RA 7659 carried RA 8177 with it since 'the spring cannot rise higher than its source,' another on dual delegation and Delegata potestas non potest delegari, and a survey of the international trend from the 1948 Universal Declaration through the Second Optional Protocol to the 1997 Commission on Human Rights resolution, concluding that 'the right to life [is] not subject to popular vote'

His own closing reflections: the dissenters will remain vigilant and will eventually win; death is too final and too irreversible a penalty; conviction in rape cases usually rests on the say-so of the offended party with appellate courts depending on trial judges' assessments; and judges, lawyers and prosecutors are imperfect, so a perfectly innocent man could die

stances.claim: Congress did not discharge its constitutional duty under Section 19, Article III: by merely reimposing death on the very same crimes already punishable by death, without defining heinousness or stating compelling reasons crime by crime, RA 7659 failed the two concurrent requirements the Charter imposes.
stances.rhetorical_move: reproduces the 32-page dissent's textual and constitutional-history argument, citing Commissioner Monsod's 'organized murder' example and a three-part test of heinousness

stances.claim: A justice may keep casting a negative vote in every death case even after the majority has ruled: review is de novo, the constitutionality of the law is an indispensable issue in each case, and duty to the Court, the country, conscience and God requires speaking out.
stances.rhetorical_move: reproduces the Escala dissent verbatim, answering the colleagues' request for unanimity with an appeal to conscience and to the nature of automatic review

stances.claim: The death penalty is not per se objectionable, but it should be prescribed only for a very limited number of truly heinous crimes and only under exceptional circumstances, because judges, lawyers and prosecutors are imperfect and an innocent man could be executed -- a risk sharpest in rape cases resting on the testimony of two persons.
stances.rhetorical_move: moves from doctrine to institutional humility, conceding the abstract permissibility of the penalty in order to press the irreversibility argument

stances.claim: When the appellant escapes, the Court should not dismiss the appeal from a death sentence, but neither should it deliberate or render judgment until the accused is rearrested or voluntarily submits to its jurisdiction.
stances.rhetorical_move: stakes out a middle position between the majority and the dissenters, joining only in the result

stances.claim: The dissenters will eventually win -- either the Court will change its mind about the constitutionality of RA 7659 or Congress will repeal or modify it.
stances.rhetorical_move: prediction offered as belief, closing the chapter on a forward-looking note

notable_anecdotes: His explanation that he must write about death cases without naming anyone, because by Court tradition such decisions and opinions are per curiam -- a practice he personally disagrees with but is bound to follow.
His commendation, in a footnote, of the FLAG lawyers for their grit and perseverance in fighting for death row convicts, naming each member of the Anti-Death Penalty Task Force.
The mundane origin of the Lethal Injection Law: the old electric chair was destroyed by fire and building a gas chamber was deemed too expensive, so Congress switched the mode of execution.

The scene inside the Court in People v. Escala, where the overwhelming majority asked a dissenter to stop voting against death so a unanimous vote could be had, and he refused after soul-searching, reflection and prayer.

The negotiated settlement of that quarrel: a final Dissenting Opinion in the Escala text plus a standard clause, reproduced in every later affirmation, recording that four members maintain the law is unconstitutional yet submit to the majority.

His arithmetic of alarm: with about 600 death cases decided and thirty more arriving monthly, affirming even half would put one convict to death every working day, giving the Philippines and the Court 'the dubious distinction of being the worst judicial killers in this world.'

one_paragraph_summary: Chapter 4 of 'Battles in the Supreme Court' recounted the Court's battles over capital punishment, written under the constraint that death-penalty decisions are per curiam, so CJP named neither ponentes nor dissenters. He set out Section 19, Article III, which permits death only for compelling reasons involving heinous crimes, and RA 7659, under which trial courts had imposed at least 748 death sentences by October 1998. In Echegaray the Court upheld the law 12 to 3, reasoning that death is not cruel or unusual, that the covered offenses are heinous, that the statute contains safeguards, and that no statistical proof of rising crime is required. He reproduced the two dissents at length, especially a 32-page opinion arguing that Congress merely made penalties more severe for crimes already punishable by death, that the framers had in mind organized murder or the brutal murder of a rape victim, that heinousness requires new offenses or new aggravating elements, that no empirical proof links death to deterrence, that the Charter shows an explosion of concern for man more than property, and that the penalty falls hardest on the poor and unlettered, closing with Scripture and Evangelium Vitae. He then traced Esparas and Prades on whether an escaped appellant's sentence must still be reviewed and judgment rendered, recording his own middle position of review without judgment until rearrest. He described the quarrel over repetitive dissents in Escala, settled by a standard clause reproduced in all later affirmations, and printed that dissent in full, with its warning of one execution every working day. He summarized the 10-4 ruling sustaining the Lethal Injection Law while voiding two implementing rules, and the dissents on dual delegation and the international abolition trend. He closed by predicting the dissenters would eventually win and warning that an innocent man could die through plain human error.
